authoredSolutions.31: Propyne with \(NaNH_{2}\) gives the acetylide \(CH_{3}-C\equiv C-Na\), which alkylates the primary carbon of \(Br-CH_{2}CH_{2}CH(OH)CH_{3}\) by \(S_{N}2\), so \(B = CH_{3}-C\equiv C-CH_{2}CH_{2}CH(OH)CH_{3}\), a seven-carbon secondary alcohol. \(H_{2}/Pd-C\) is an unpoisoned catalyst, so the triple bond is reduced all the way to the alkane and \(C\) is heptan-2-ol. \(CrO_{3}\) oxidises a secondary alcohol to a ketone, so \(D\) is heptan-2-one, \(CH_{3}CH_{2}CH_{2}CH_{2}CH_{2}COCH_{3}\). Option (A) is hexanal, which would require one carbon fewer and a primary alcohol, while options (B) and (C) still contain a \(C=C\) that \(H_{2}/Pd-C\) would have removed. The answer is option (D).
authoredSolutions.32: \(NaOCl\) followed by \(H_{3}O^{+}\) is the haloform reaction: it converts a methyl ketone \(R-CO-CH_{3}\) into the carboxylic acid \(R-COOH\), the methyl carbon leaving as \(CHCl_{3}\). The product drawn is but-2-enoic acid, \(CH_{3}-CH=CH-COOH\), so \(R = CH_{3}-CH=CH-\) and \(P\) must be the methyl ketone \(CH_{3}-CH=CH-CO-CH_{3}\) (pent-3-en-2-one), option (A). Option (B), pent-2-enal, is an aldehyde and would be oxidised with no loss of carbon; options (C) and (D), a cyclic enol ether and cyclopentanone, carry no \(CO-CH_{3}\) group at all. The answer is option (A).
authoredSolutions.33: Xenon brings 8 valence electrons; each \(Xe-F\) single bond uses one of them and each \(Xe=O\) double bond uses two, and whatever remains stays as lone pairs. \(XeF_{2}\): \(8-2 = 6\) electrons, i.e. 3 lone pairs, matching (iv). \(XeO_{2}F_{2}\): \(8-(2\times 2)-(2\times 1) = 2\), i.e. 1 lone pair, matching (ii). \(XeO_{3}F_{2}\): \(8-(3\times 2)-(2\times 1) = 0\), i.e. no lone pair, matching (i). \(XeF_{4}\): \(8-4 = 4\), i.e. 2 lone pairs, matching (iii). The set (A)-(iv), (B)-(ii), (C)-(i), (D)-(iii) is option (D).
authoredSolutions.34: Back donation puts a filled halogen \(p\) orbital into the empty \(2p\) orbital on boron, so its strength is decided by how well the two orbitals overlap. Fluorine donates from a \(2p\) orbital, giving \(2p\pi-2p\pi\) overlap with boron's own \(2p\); chlorine, bromine and iodine must use \(3p\), \(4p\) and \(5p\) orbitals, which are larger and more diffuse and match boron's compact \(2p\) progressively worse. Back donation therefore falls in the order \(BF_{3} > BCl_{3} > BBr_{3} > BI_{3}\), which is also why \(BF_{3}\) is the weakest Lewis acid of the four. The answer is option (B).
authoredSolutions.35: Deuterium has twice the mass of protium, so the \(D-D\) bond has a lower zero-point energy and hence a higher bond dissociation enthalpy than \(H-H\) (about \(443\) against \(436\text{ }kJ\text{ }mol^{-1}\)). Because that bond must break in the rate-determining step, \(D_{2}\) reacts more slowly than \(H_{2}\) — the kinetic isotope effect. Deuterium is a stable isotope and emits no \(\beta^{+}\) particles, so option (D) is wrong as well. The answer is option (A).
authoredSolutions.36: Liquation exploits a large gap in melting points: the impure metal is heated on a sloping hearth to just above its own melting point, so the metal runs off while the higher-melting impurities are left behind. It is therefore the method for low melting metals such as tin, lead and bismuth. Zone refining is reserved for ultrapure semiconductors like silicon and germanium, electrolytic refining for metals such as copper and aluminium, and chromatography for separating trace amounts. The answer is option (B).
authoredSolutions.37: \(NaCl\) has only paired electrons in both of its ions, so it is diamagnetic, matching (iii). \(Fe_{3}O_{4}\) (magnetite) contains \(Fe^{2+}\) and \(Fe^{3+}\) whose moments align oppositely but are unequal in size, so they do not cancel and a net moment survives: ferrimagnetism, matching (iv). \(O_{2}\) carries two unpaired electrons in its \(\pi^{*}\) orbitals and is paramagnetic, matching (ii). In \(MnO\) neighbouring moments are equal and opposite and cancel exactly, which is antiferromagnetism, matching (i). The set (A)-(iii), (B)-(iv), (C)-(ii), (D)-(i) is option (C).
authoredSolutions.38: Structure (A) is morphine and structure (D) is its \(3\)-methyl ether codeine; both are narcotic analgesics, which kills option (A) (it calls diazepam an analgesic) and option (C) (it calls morphine and codeine tranquillisers). Structure (B) is diazepam, a benzodiazepine tranquilliser, and structure (C) is serotonin, the neurotransmitter whose depleted level tranquillisers act to restore and which is treated alongside them in the syllabus. Option (B) fails because it sweeps codeine in with the tranquillisers. Only option (D) survives, and it is the official answer.
authoredSolutions.39: Alcoholic \(NH_{3}\) converts the acid chloride \((CH_{3})_{2}CHCH_{2}CH_{2}COCl\) into the corresponding amide. \(NaOH/Br_{2}\) is the Hofmann bromamide degradation, which expels the carbonyl carbon and delivers a primary amine with one carbon fewer, \((CH_{3})_{2}CHCH_{2}CH_{2}NH_{2}\). \(NaNO_{2}/HCl\) diazotises this primary aliphatic amine and water then displaces \(N_{2}\), giving the alcohol with the same skeleton, \((CH_{3})_{2}CHCH_{2}CH_{2}OH\) or 3-methylbutan-1-ol. Option (B) retains all six carbons and so misses the degradation step, while (A) and (D) invent a halogen that nothing in the sequence can install. The answer is option (C).
authoredSolutions.40: A primary amine has two \(N-H\) bonds while a secondary amine has only one, so a primary amine can donate two hydrogen bonds and its intermolecular association is greater, not less. Statement (A) reverses this and is therefore the one that is not correct. The other three are true: primary aliphatic amines other than methylamine give the corresponding alcohols with nitrous acid, secondary aliphatic amines are more basic than primary ones in water because of the extra electron-releasing alkyl group, and the Gabriel phthalimide route is a standard preparation of pure primary amines. The answer is option (A).
authoredSolutions.41: Prussian blue exists in two forms. When \(Fe^{3+}\) is in excess the insoluble form \(Fe_{4}[Fe(CN)_{6}]_{3}\) is thrown down as a precipitate. When potassium ferrocyanide is in excess, as specified here, ferrocyanide ions are adsorbed on the surface of the particles and \(K^{+}\) ions are taken up to balance the charge, giving the peptised soluble form \(KFe[Fe(CN)_{6}]\), which stays dispersed as a colloid. Since the question asks for the colloidal species formed with excess \(K_{4}[Fe(CN)_{6}]\), the answer is option (D).
authoredSolutions.42: A gas that is unreactive, non-toxic and non-flammable, and so survives the troposphere and drifts up into the stratosphere, is a chlorofluorocarbon such as \(CF_{2}Cl_{2}\) (freon-12). In the stratosphere UV radiation breaks its weakest bond, \(C-Cl\), homolytically: \(CF_{2}Cl_{2} \rightarrow \dot{C}l + \dot{C}F_{2}Cl\). The much stronger \(C-F\) bond is untouched, a \(\dot{C}H_{3}\) fragment is impossible because the molecule contains no hydrogen, and \(Cl\dot{O}\) appears only later, when the chlorine radical attacks ozone. The pair formed initially is therefore \(\dot{C}l\) and \(\dot{C}F_{2}Cl\), option (D).
authoredSolutions.43: Gypsum is \(CaSO_{4}\cdot 2H_{2}O\), so it carries 2 molecules of water. Heating it to about \(393\text{ }K\) drives off most of that water and leaves plaster of Paris, \(CaSO_{4}\cdot \frac{1}{2}H_{2}O\), with \(0.5\). Heating beyond about \(473\text{ }K\) removes the remainder completely and gives dead burnt plaster, anhydrous \(CaSO_{4}\), with 0. Taken in the order the question asks, gypsum then dead burnt plaster then plaster of Paris, the values are 2, 0 and \(0.5\), which is option (D).
authoredSolutions.44: For a transition metal the acidic character of an oxide grows with the oxidation state of the metal: low states give basic oxides, intermediate states amphoteric ones and high states acidic ones. Vanadium is in the \(+3\) state in \(V_{2}O_{3}\) and chromium is in the \(+2\) state in \(CrO\), both low, so both oxides are basic. The contrast is instructive, since the same two metals give amphoteric \(V_{2}O_{4}\) and \(Cr_{2}O_{3}\) and strongly acidic \(V_{2}O_{5}\) and \(CrO_{3}\) at higher oxidation states. Hence \(X\) and \(Y\) are both basic, option (D).
authoredSolutions.45: Uracil can be drawn in a diketo (lactam) form and in enol (lactim) tautomers, in which one or both carbonyls become \(-OH\) and the corresponding ring \(N-H\) is lost. The base actually present in RNA is the diketo form, carrying \(C=O\) at both position 2 and position 4 and an \(N-H\) at both \(N1\) and \(N3\); this is the arrangement that supplies the donor and acceptor sites needed to hydrogen bond with adenine. Options (A), (B) and (C) are the di-enol and the two mono-enol tautomers, which are only minor forms. The answer is option (D).
authoredSolutions.46: Williamson synthesis needs an alkoxide or phenoxide and a partner halide that can undergo \(S_{N}2\). Ethyl phenyl ether is indeed made this way, from sodium phenoxide and ethyl bromide, so the assertion is correct. The reason reverses the roles: bromobenzene is an aryl halide whose \(C-Br\) bond has partial double bond character through resonance, and its \(sp^{2}\) carbon cannot be attacked from behind, so ethoxide does not displace bromide and no ether is formed. Assertion correct, reason wrong, which is option (B).
authoredSolutions.47: Chlorocyclopentane with magnesium in dry ether gives the Grignard reagent \(A\), cyclopentylmagnesium chloride, in which the ring carbon bears a large negative charge and behaves as a carbanion. Ethanol has an acidic \(O-H\) proton, so it simply protonates that carbanion: the Grignard is destroyed and the hydrocarbon cyclopentane is released along with \(C_{2}H_{5}OMgCl\). This is exactly why Grignard reagents must be prepared under strictly anhydrous, proton-free conditions. No ether forms, no ethyl group is coupled on and no elimination occurs, so options (B), (C) and (D) fail. The answer is option (A).
authoredSolutions.48: In the van der Waals equation the internal pressure term \(an^{2}/V^{2}\) is added to \(P\), so it must itself have the units of pressure. Rearranging, \(a = PV^{2}/n^{2}\). With pressure in \(atm\), volume in \(dm^{3}\) and amount in \(mol\), this gives \(atm\text{ }dm^{6}\text{ }mol^{-2}\). Option (B), \(dm^{3}\text{ }mol^{-1}\), is the unit of the excluded volume parameter \(b\), which is subtracted from \(V\) rather than added to \(P\). The answer is option (D).
authoredSolutions.49: A polythionic acid \(H_{2}S_{x}O_{6}\) is built as \(HO_{3}S-(S)_{x-2}-SO_{3}H\): two terminal sulphur atoms each carrying three oxygens, joined through a catenated chain of bare sulphur atoms. A terminal sulphur is bonded to three oxygens and one sulphur, and a bond between like atoms contributes nothing to oxidation state, so it is \(+5\). Each chain sulphur is flanked only by sulphur, so it is 0. The values present are therefore 0 and \(+5\), option (D). Averaging the charge over all \(x\) sulphur atoms instead would give a meaningless fraction, which is the trap here.
authoredSolutions.50: The Tyndall effect is the scattering of light by particles whose size is comparable to the wavelength of light, roughly \(1\) to \(1000\text{ }nm\). A true solution has particles far too small to scatter, and a suspension has particles so large that it blocks light rather than showing a scattered cone. Both sols lie in the colloidal range, but in a lyophilic sol the dispersed phase is heavily solvated and its refractive index is close to that of the medium, which weakens the scattering; a lyophobic sol has a sharp refractive index difference from the medium and so scatters strongly. The answer is option (C).
authoredSolutions.51: \(AgBr\) has molar mass \(108 + 80 = 188\text{ }g\text{ }mol^{-1}\), so \(0.188\text{ }g\) of it is \(0.188/188 = 1.0\times 10^{-3}\text{ }mol\). In the Carius method every bromine atom of the organic compound is precipitated as one \(AgBr\), so the sample contains \(1.0\times 10^{-3}\text{ }mol\) of bromine, that is \(1.0\times 10^{-3}\times 80 = 0.08\text{ }g\). The percentage of bromine is therefore \((0.08/0.2)\times 100 = 40\%\). The answer is 40.
authoredSolutions.52: Rates of different species in one reaction can only be equated after each is divided by its own stoichiometric coefficient. Here ethanol has coefficient 3 and \(Cr_{2}(SO_{4})_{3}\) has coefficient 2, so \(-\frac{1}{3}\frac{d[C_{2}H_{6}O]}{dt} = \frac{1}{2}\frac{d[Cr_{2}(SO_{4})_{3}]}{dt}\). Substituting the given rate of appearance gives a rate of disappearance of ethanol equal to \(\frac{3}{2}\times 2.67 = 4.005\text{ }mol\text{ }min^{-1}\). To the nearest integer the answer is 4.
authoredSolutions.53: Bohr quantisation gives \(mvr = nh/2\pi\), so \(v = nh/(2\pi mr)\) and the kinetic energy is \(\frac{1}{2}mv^{2} = \frac{n^{2}h^{2}}{8\pi^{2}mr^{2}}\). For hydrogen the orbit radius is \(r = n^{2}a_{0}\), so for the second orbit \(n = 2\) and \(r = 4a_{0}\), giving \(KE = \frac{4h^{2}}{8\pi^{2}m(4a_{0})^{2}} = \frac{h^{2}}{32\pi^{2}ma_{0}^{2}}\). Comparing with \(h^{2}/(xma_{0}^{2})\) gives \(x = 32\pi^{2} = 32\times (3.14)^{2} = 315.51\), so \(10x = 3155.1\). To the nearest integer the answer is 3155.
authoredSolutions.54: Let the \(1000\text{ }g\) of solution contain \(w\) grams of water, leaving \((1000-w)\) grams of sucrose, i.e. \((1000-w)/342\) mol. A molality of \(0.75\) requires \(\frac{(1000-w)/342}{w/1000} = 0.75\), giving \(1000(1000-w) = 256.5w\) and \(w = 795.86\text{ }g\), so the sucrose present is \(0.5969\text{ }mol\). Freezing removes solvent but not solute, so the residual solution still holds all \(0.5969\text{ }mol\) while its water falls to \(a\) kg. At the limiting temperature \(\Delta T_{f} = 4 = 1.86\times \frac{0.5969}{a}\), so \(a = 0.2776\text{ }kg = 277.6\text{ }g\). The ice separated is \(795.86 - 277.6 = 518.3\text{ }g\), which to the nearest integer is 518.
authoredSolutions.55: Only chloride outside the coordination sphere is free to be precipitated by \(AgNO_{3}\). One mole of complex yielding one mole of \(AgCl\) therefore means exactly one ionisable \(Cl^{-}\), so the complex is \([MCl_{2}L_{2}]Cl\) with the other two chlorides coordinated. Since the geometry is octahedral there are six coordination sites, shared between the two coordinated chlorides and the two \(L\) molecules: \(2 + 2d = 6\), where \(d\) is the denticity of \(L\). Hence \(d = 2\) and \(L\) is bidentate. The answer is 2.
authoredSolutions.56: \(N,N\)-dimethylaminopentane is \(C_{7}H_{17}N\), of molar mass \(7(12) + 17 + 14 = 115\text{ }g\text{ }mol^{-1}\), so \(57.5\text{ }g\) is \(0.5\text{ }mol\). In Dumas estimation the \(CuO\) supplies every oxygen atom needed for complete combustion: \(C_{7}H_{17}N + \frac{45}{2}CuO \rightarrow 7CO_{2} + \frac{17}{2}H_{2}O + \frac{1}{2}N_{2} + \frac{45}{2}Cu\), the coefficient following from the oxygen balance \(7(2) + \frac{17}{2} = 22.5\). Therefore \(n_{CuO} = 22.5\times 0.5 = 11.25\), which is \(1125\times 10^{-2}\). The answer is 1125.
authoredSolutions.57: Neptunium, \(Z = 93\), is the actinoid immediately after uranium, and its ground state configuration is \([Rn]5f^{4}6d^{1}7s^{2}\). In the early actinoids the \(5f\) and \(6d\) levels lie very close in energy, so one electron occupies \(6d\) rather than all five entering \(5f\). Counting only the \(f\) subshell gives 4 electrons. The answer is 4.
authoredSolutions.58: The millimoles of \(HCl\) are \(200\times 0.2 = 40\) and of \(NaOH\) are \(300\times 0.1 = 30\), so \(NaOH\) is limiting and only \(0.030\text{ }mol\) of water is formed. The heat released is \(0.030\times 57.1\text{ }kJ = 1713\text{ }J\). With no volume change on mixing the solution mass is \(500\text{ }mL\times 1.00\text{ }g\text{ }cm^{-3} = 500\text{ }g\), so \(\Delta T = \frac{q}{mc} = \frac{1713}{500\times 4.18} = 0.8196\text{ }K\), that is \(81.96\times 10^{-2}\). To the nearest integer \(x = 82\).
authoredSolutions.59: Let \(a\) mol of \(NH_{3}\) be added to \(2\text{ }L\), so its initial concentration is \(a/2\) while \([Ag^{+}]_{0} = 0.80\text{ }M\). Because \(K_{f} = 1.0\times 10^{8}\) is very large, \(Ag^{+} + 2NH_{3} \rightleftharpoons [Ag(NH_{3})_{2}]^{+}\) runs essentially to completion: the complex reaches \(0.80\text{ }M\), ammonia is consumed to the extent of \(1.60\text{ }M\), and the free ammonia left is \((a/2 - 1.60)\). Substituting into \(K_{f} = \frac{0.80}{(5.0\times 10^{-8})(a/2 - 1.60)^{2}} = 1.0\times 10^{8}\) gives \((a/2 - 1.60)^{2} = 0.16\), hence \(a/2 - 1.60 = 0.40\) and \(a = 4\). The answer is 4.
authoredSolutions.60: In acidic medium \(MnO_{4}^{-}\) is reduced to \(Mn^{2+}\), a five-electron change, while \(Fe^{2+}\) is oxidised to \(Fe^{3+}\), a one-electron change, so the n-factors are 5 and 1. Equating equivalents for the equal \(10\text{ }mL\) volumes, \(5\times M\times 10 = 1\times 0.1\times 10\), which gives \(M = 0.02\text{ }M\). The molar mass of \(KMnO_{4}\) is \(39 + 55 + 4(16) = 158\text{ }g\text{ }mol^{-1}\), so the strength is \(0.02\times 158 = 3.16\text{ }g\text{ }L^{-1}\), that is \(316\times 10^{-2}\). The answer is 316.
authoredSolutions.80: The hexagon has perimeter \(6s\), so the square has perimeter \(20-6s\) and side \(\frac{10-3s}{2}\). The combined area is \(A=\left(\frac{10-3s}{2}\right)^{2}+\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{2}s^{2}\). Setting \(\frac{dA}{ds}=-\frac{3(10-3s)}{2}+3\sqrt{3}\,s=0\) gives \(2\sqrt{3}\,s=10-3s\), so \(s=\frac{10}{3+2\sqrt{3}}\). Since \(\frac{d^{2}A}{ds^{2}}>0\), this is the minimum. Hence (D).
authoredSolutions.85: Completing the square, \(x^{2}+x+1=\left(x+\tfrac12\right)^{2}+\tfrac34\). With \(u=x+\tfrac12,\ k=\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\), \(\int\frac{du}{(u^{2}+k^{2})^{2}}=\frac{1}{2k^{2}}\left[\frac{u}{u^{2}+k^{2}}+\frac1k\tan^{-1}\frac{u}{k}\right]\) gives \(a=\frac{4}{3\sqrt3}\) and \(b=\frac13\). Hence \(9(\sqrt3\,a+b)=9\left(\frac43+\frac13\right)=15\).
authoredSolutions.89: A six-digit palindrome \(\overline{abccba}\) (with \(a\neq0\)) is automatically divisible by 11, since its alternating digit sum is \(a-b+c-c+b-a=0\). Divisibility by 5 needs the last digit \(a\in\{0,5\}\); as \(a\neq0\), \(a=5\). With \(b,c\) each free (10 ways), the count is \(10\times10=100\).
